overview:
Nandīśvara (often called Nandīśvaradvīpa) is a sacred continent in Jain cosmology, located in the madhyaloka, the middle world of the Jain universe. It forms one of the concentric island-continents that surround Mount Meru and is encircled by the ocean known as Nandīśvaroda (Nandīśvarodasamudra). While humans can be born only in the middle world, Nandīśvara itself is described as a realm inaccessible to human beings and specially associated with the gods (devas) and their worship of the Tīrthaṅkaras.

In both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, Nandīśvara is portrayed as a land of divine delight, filled with gardens, lotus-lakes, and temples dedicated to the Jinas. Classical cosmological texts such as the Saṃgrahaṇīratna (Śvetāmbara), Tiloyapaṇṇatti and Trilokasāra (Digambara), and narrative works like Hemacandra’s "Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra" give detailed descriptions of its geography and sacred architecture. The continent is said to surround Mount Meru with an immense diameter measured in yojanas, and to be bordered by the Nandīśvaroda ocean, forming the eighth island in the series of concentric dvīpas.

At the center of Nandīśvara stand four Añjana mountains, placed in the cardinal directions—Devaramaṇa in the east, Nityodyata in the south, Svayamprabha in the west, and Ramaṇīya in the north. These mountains are described as dark or antimony-colored and of great height, sometimes compared to smaller Merus. On their summits are magnificent temples (caityas) of the Arhats, with multiple doors, jeweled platforms, and richly adorned altars. Within these temples are eternal images (śāśvata-bimba) of certain Tīrthaṅkaras—commonly Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna (Mahāvīra), Candrānana, and Vāriṣeṇa—each represented in meditation posture and attended by divine retinues of Nāgas, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and other celestial beings.

Surrounding the Añjana mountains are numerous lotus-lakes, each with its own name and characteristics, and beyond them vast gardens filled with trees such as Aśoka, Saptacchadaka, Campaka, and Cūta (mango). The lakes are described as square, deep, bordered by jeweled embankments, and full of clear water. The gardens are said to stretch for thousands of yojanas, providing a setting for the gods’ worship and enjoyment. The entire continent is thus envisioned as a cosmic pilgrimage site where devas perform elaborate pūjā to the Jinas, using incense, garlands, auspicious symbols, banners, umbrellas, and other ritual objects.

In ritual and festival practice, Nandīśvara plays a central symbolic role, especially in the observance of Aṣṭāhnika (Aṣṭāhnika Parva). During specific eight-day periods in the months of Āṣāḍha, Kārtika, and Phālguna, it is believed that gods from various heavenly realms gather on Nandīśvara to worship the Tīrthaṅkaras in its temples. Because humans cannot physically reach Nandīśvara, they perform symbolic worship of Nandīśvara images or temples on earth, aligning their devotion with the celestial worship taking place in the cosmic realm. This practice is understood to inspire feelings of detachment (vairāgya) and spiritual aspiration in lay followers.

Theologically, Nandīśvara illustrates several key Jain ideas: the vastness and structured order of the universe; the continuity of Tīrthaṅkara worship across realms; and the notion that ideal, eternal temples and images exist beyond human history. The "akr̥trima" (non-artificial, beginningless) temples of Nandīśvara are said to have existed since time immemorial, emphasizing that the veneration of the Jinas is not merely a human cultural construct but a cosmic reality. At the same time, the inaccessibility of Nandīśvara to humans underscores the limits of human embodiment and the need for symbolic, meditative participation in the wider spiritual universe.

Across Jain communities today, Nandīśvara continues to be a powerful imaginative and devotional focus. Temples and icons representing Nandīśvara-dvīpa—often showing Mount Meru surrounded by concentric islands and oceans, with Nandīśvara marked as a special ring—serve as visual aids for cosmological contemplation and ritual worship. These representations bridge scriptural cosmology and lived practice, allowing devotees to situate their own acts of pūjā within the grand architecture of the Jain cosmos.

primary_sources.title: Saṃgrahaṇīratna
primary_sources.author: Śrīcandra (Śvetāmbara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text: नन्दीश्वरद्वीपः मध्यलोके स्थितो द्वीपविशेषः, नन्दीश्वरोदसमुद्रेण परिवृतः। अयं जम्बूद्वीपाद्यष्टमो द्वीपः, मेरुं परितः परिवर्तते। देवानां रम्यभूमिरयं, तत्र जिनेन्द्रपूजायां नित्यनिरताः सुराः।
primary_sources.transliteration: nandīśvaradvīpaḥ madhyaloke sthito dvīpaviśeṣaḥ, nandīśvarodasamudreṇa parivṛtaḥ. ayaṃ jambūdvīpādy aṣṭamo dvīpaḥ, meruṃ paritaḥ parivartate. devānāṃ ramyabhūmir ayaṃ, tatra jinendrapūjāyāṃ nityaniratāḥ surāḥ.
primary_sources.translation: Nandīśvara-dvīpa is a special continent situated in the middle world, surrounded by the ocean called Nandīśvaroda. It is the eighth continent, following Jambūdvīpa and the others, and it encircles Mount Meru. This is a delightful land of the gods, where the deities are constantly engaged in the worship of the Jinas.
primary_sources.notes: This passage summarizes the cosmological placement of Nandīśvara within the concentric dvīpas of madhyaloka and emphasizes its association with divine worship. The Saṃgrahaṇīratna is a Śvetāmbara cosmological compendium that systematizes earlier canonical descriptions.

primary_sources.title: Tiloyapaṇṇatti
primary_sources.author: Yativṛṣabha (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text:
आदीदो खलु अट्ठमणंदीसरदीववलयविक्खंभो सयसमहियतेवट्ठीकोडी चुलसीदिलक्खा ये।
एक्कचउक्कट्ठं जणदहिमुहरइयरणगा पडिदिसम्हि मज्झे चउदिसवावीमज्झे तब्बाहिरदुकोणे।
primary_sources.transliteration:
ādīdo khalu aṭṭhamaṇandīsaradvīvavalayavikkhaṃbho sayasamahiyatevaṭṭhīkoḍī culasīdilakkhā ye.
ekkacaukkatthaṃ jaṇadahimuharaiyaraṇagā paḍidisamhi majjhe caudisavāvīmajjhe tabbāhiradukoṇe.
primary_sources.translation: From the beginning, indeed, the circumference of the eighth Nandīśvara-dvīpa is measured as one hundred and sixty-three crore and eighty-four lakh yojanas. In each direction there are, in the middle, four lakes, and in the middle of these four directions, at the outer corners, there are mountains named Añjana, Dadhimukha, and Ratikara.
primary_sources.notes: The Tiloyapaṇṇatti, a Prakrit cosmological text, gives precise measurements and spatial arrangements for Nandīśvara, including the number and placement of mountains and lakes. The quoted verses form part of a longer description of the dvīpa’s geography and sacred structures.

primary_sources.title: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra (Ajitanātha-caritra, Part: Description of Nandīśvara)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandra
primary_sources.original_text: तत्र मध्यभागे चत्वारोऽञ्जनपर्वताः कज्जलवर्णा देवरमणो दक्षिणे नित्योद्यातः, पश्चिमे स्वयम्प्रभः, उत्तरस्यां रमणीयः। तेषां शिखरेषु जिनालयाः शतयोजनदीर्घाः, तदर्धविस्तीर्णाः, सप्ततियोजनोन्नताः, चतुर्द्वारयुक्ताः। तेषु मणिपीठिकासु चतुःषोडशयोजनदीर्घविस्तीर्णासु, अष्टयोजनोन्नतासु, देवचन्दकाः सर्वरत्नमयाः, तेषु च शाश्वतबिम्बानि ऋषभवर्धमानचन्द्राननवारिषेणानां पर्याṅकस्थितानां।
primary_sources.transliteration: tatra madhyabhāge catvāro 'ñjanaparvataḥ kajjalavarṇā devaramaṇo dakṣiṇe nityodyātaḥ, paścime svayamprabhaḥ, uttarasyaṃ ramaṇīyaḥ. teṣāṃ śikhareṣu jinalayāḥ śatayojanadīrghāḥ, tadardhavistīrṇāḥ, saptatiyojanonnatāḥ, caturdvārayuktāḥ. teṣu maṇipīṭhikāsu catuḥṣoḍaśayojanadīrghavistīrṇāsu, aṣṭayojanonnatāsu, devacandakāḥ sarvaratnamayāḥ, teṣu ca śāśvatabimbāni ṛṣabhavardhamānacandrānana vāriṣeṇānāṃ paryaṅkasthitānām.
primary_sources.translation: There, in the central region, are four Añjana mountains, dark like collyrium: Devaramaṇa in the east, Nityodyata in the south, Svayamprabha in the west, and Ramaṇīya in the north. On their summits are temples of the Jinas, one hundred yojanas in length, half as wide, and seventy yojanas high, each furnished with four doors. Within them, on jeweled platforms sixteen yojanas long and wide and eight yojanas high, are altars of jewels, and upon these are eternal images of the Arhats Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, Candrānana, and Vāriṣeṇa, seated in the meditation posture.
primary_sources.notes: Hemacandra’s Sanskrit narrative work elaborates the cosmological description with rich architectural and devotional detail. The passage highlights the four Añjana mountains, the dimensions of the temples, and the presence of eternal Tīrthaṅkara images, reinforcing Nandīśvara’s status as a divine pilgrimage site.

primary_sources.title: Trilokasāra
primary_sources.author: Nemichandra Siddhānta Cakravartin (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text: मध्यलोके नन्दीश्वरद्वीपः नन्दीश्वरोदसमुद्रेण परिवृतः, मेरुं परितो वलयाकारः। तत्र देवाः जिनपूजायां निरताः, मानुषाणां तु तत्रागमनं नास्ति।
primary_sources.transliteration: madhyaloke nandīśvaradvīpaḥ nandīśvarodasamudreṇa parivṛtaḥ, meruṃ parito valayākāraḥ. tatra devāḥ jinapūjāyāṃ niratāḥ, mānuṣāṇāṃ tu tatrāgamanaṃ nāsti.
primary_sources.translation: In the middle world, the Nandīśvara continent is encircled by the Nandīśvaroda ocean, forming a ring around Meru. There the gods are engaged in the worship of the Jinas, but for human beings there is no possibility of going there.
primary_sources.notes: The Trilokasāra is a concise Sanskrit treatise on the three worlds. This passage underscores both the centrality of Nandīśvara in divine worship and its inaccessibility to humans, a key doctrinal point that shapes later ritual symbolism.

misconceptions.myth: Humans can physically travel to Nandīśvara-dvīpa through extraordinary ascetic practice or advanced technology.
misconceptions.reality: Jain cosmological texts consistently state that Nandīśvara is beyond human reach. It is a realm where gods worship the Tīrthaṅkaras, and humans participate only symbolically through images, rituals, and meditation. No scriptural source supports the idea of bodily travel to Nandīśvara.

misconceptions.myth: Nandīśvara is a historical geographic location on Earth that can be identified with a specific mountain range or island.
misconceptions.reality: Nandīśvara belongs to the structured cosmology of the Jain universe, not to ordinary terrestrial geography. Although some earthly temples visually represent Nandīśvara and Mount Meru, these are symbolic constructions, not literal maps of a physical place on Earth.

misconceptions.myth: The temples of Nandīśvara were built by human architects at some point in cosmic history.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts describe the Nandīśvara temples as "akr̥trima"—non-artificial and beginningless. They are said to exist eternally as part of the cosmic order, emphasizing that Tīrthaṅkara worship transcends human historical construction.

misconceptions.myth: Only one Tīrthaṅkara is associated with Nandīśvara, usually Mahāvīra, and the other Jinas are absent.
misconceptions.reality: Primary sources describe multiple Tīrthaṅkaras—such as Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna (Mahāvīra), Candrānana, and Vāriṣeṇa—having eternal images in the Nandīśvara temples. The continent is a collective site of worship for several Jinas, not exclusively dedicated to a single figure.
